toc.title: Look at what's going on around that time

blocks.p: If you've been through a panic attack, you know that they are no joke. You might go through panic attacks repeatedly, or even at the same time every day, like at night.

That's where this started: with a question from one of my community members: "I tend to get dysregulated pretty much every night, come around 10 o'clock. Do you get ahead of it? What are your thoughts to help me?"
Here's how I'd work with that, to reduce both the intensity and the frequency, through passive and active means, focused on the Polyvagal safety state.
Getting ahead of it is always a really good idea. Always, always, always. If you know that you get dysregulated at a certain time, then it's probably a good idea to prepare for that ahead of time.

Maybe there's some sort of ritual you need to set up right before that time: exercising, slowing down, drinking tea or something warm. Maybe there's something you can do to help slow down, depending on what kind of dysregulation you have.
Wherever you're at during that time, if that's bedtime, set up that environment to provide you more passive cues of safety than not. That helps lay the foundation of safety.
On top of that, there might be an active safety anchor you can use: yoga, drinking something warm, deep breathing, fidgeting, having the right music on, having silence. Whatever it is for you.
So ask yourself two things. What can I surround myself with? And what can I actively do to help slow down, to be more regulated, to feel more calm and at peace in the present moment?

blocks.h: Look at what's going on around that time

blocks.p: You can also look at the context of the situation and ask, "What the heck is going on around this time that I can address?"

You can do that in the moment. At 9:55, ask yourself, "Okay, here I am. How am I doing?" Then look around and notice: is there anything here that clearly sends me more into dysregulation than into safety?

Maybe I don't do well with the dark. Maybe I'm okay in my room, but I can see out the door, and there's a dark hallway, and that does something for me. So maybe I put on a small light, or I put the hall light on.

You can also reflect on the past. Think about last night and ask yourself, "What was going on before this and during this that I can address and start to change, to set myself up for more passive cues of safety?"

Maybe it's something that builds up the entire day, and the issue isn't 10 o'clock at night. Maybe the issue is that at the end of my workday, I never give myself the solitude I need to slow down and read a book, or whatever it is. So the issue might be earlier in the day, when I never gave myself what I needed. It could be a bunch of things. You have to trace your footsteps.
Setting up all that safety is the go-to. Then, in the moment itself, there are three passes:

ol: Anchor in safety, then allow the dysregulation as much as you can tolerate, and feel it.

blocks.p: A follow-up question came next: "How do you handle it when you're in the middle of some of those adaptive behaviors, and you really want to pull yourself out, but you're having a hard time?"
One thing you can do is just let it be there. Don't fight it. It's there. "I see you." One member had a wonderful top-down reframe for this: this is adaptive.

So you let it be there, and you say, "Okay, you're here with me. Cool. You're welcome to hang out with me in my pocket, but I'm also going to go do something to ground myself in safety." That's the second pass: safety anchoring, or a coping skill.

If you have enough anchoring in your system, you can take the third pass. Start top-down: validate, normalize, and give permission. Then allow the emotion, through the AWE method: allow, witness, experience. Even if you can only do the allow and witness part, that's a start.
If you can do that while grounded in safety, the intensity of the dysregulation that always happens at a certain time might soften. And the next day, it might soften even more.

When you mindfully feel it, an impulse might arise. If someone is in a really flight, anxious kind of feeling, allowing it might get them down deep enough into what they're going through that they feel an impulse to get up and move.
If they can use that impulse to move, it might not be as big of a deal the following night. Hopefully it'll be relieved, but it's not a guarantee.

On the current night, if you act on the impulse, the idea is that you can further climb your [Polyvagal ladder](piece:autonomic-nervous-system), so that the flight impulse won't be stuck. If you can act on it and use it mindfully, the ladder climbing will happen, and you'll be able to get further up into the safety state.
So if you can break that cycle, that's obviously a good thing. And if you can mindfully experience it and act on the impulse, then hopefully the stuckness will continue to ease.

blocks.why: This article talks about anchoring in safety. This practice does just that, tuned to you.
